item.title: Section 301 “excess capacity” tariffs: the US, China and Vietnam lose, the UK gains, if it stays outside
item.dc:creator: Oleksandr Shepotylo
item.description:
Today USTR proposed country-wide tariffs on 14 economies under Section 301, on the grounds of “structural excess capacity”. (My diary entry covers what is in the notices.) The obvious next question is who gains and who loses. To answer it, I built the proposed tariffs product by product and ran them through a general-equilibrium (GE) trade model of 81 economies. I also ran 5,000 Monte Carlo draws to see how robust the results are.

The short answer:

  • The US loses, in every scenario.
  • China and the Southeast Asian exporters that replaced it lose most.
  • The EU roughly breaks even on income, but more displaced Asian goods head its way.
  • The UK, which is not on the list, gains a little. That holds only for as long as it stays off the list.

Key takeaways

  • It is a top-up, not a new wall. On average the proposal adds 2.3pp to US import tariffs, mostly on China (+9.7pp) and Vietnam (+9.3pp). The EU gets about +1.6pp, and Japan and Korea less than 1pp.
  • The US loses in every scenario and in all 5,000 model runs. US real income falls by 0.03–0.06%, even after about $34bn a year of extra tariff revenue.
  • China loses 0.03–0.05%, and about twice that if talks fail and its rate rises to 40%. Vietnam (−0.5% to −0.8%) and Cambodia (−1.0% to −1.6%) lose far more.
  • The EU is roughly unaffected on income. But it faces $17–35bn of goods diverted from the US market, several times more than the UK.
  • The UK gains about £0.3–0.5bn a year (+0.010–0.016%). UK exports to the US rise by 4.5–6%. The gain is positive in every model run.
  • The gains are in mid-tech manufacturing: machinery, scientific and medical instruments, electrical equipment, chemicals and plastics. Cars, steel and most pharmaceuticals are unaffected.
  • The risk is being drawn in. If the UK were added at 20%, the gain would turn into a loss, and UK exports to the US would fall by about 5%.

A top-up, not a new wall

The key to the numbers is a detail of the notices: every proposed rate is net of existing Section 301 duties. Since 24 July 2026, 60 economies, the UK among them, have paid a forced-labour Section 301 tariff of 10–12.5%. The new action uses exactly the same core exemption list. So for most targets it only tops up the duty they already pay to the new headline rate. The UK stays where it is.

Take a product with a 2% MFN tariff that is covered by both actions:

Total US tariff (MFN + Section 301) on an illustrative covered product with 2% MFN, %. Sources: forced-labour Section 301 tiers (91 FR 47717) and the proposed rates in the USTR notices of 25 November 2026.
Exporter Today Under the proposal Gap to the UK
United Kingdom 12 12 –
EU 10 15 +3
Japan, Korea, Switzerland 12.5 15 +3
Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Cambodia 12–14.5 20 +8
China 14.5 22 +10
India 12 27 +15
Vietnam 14.5 37 +25

On covered goods, the UK goes from paying 2pp more than EU exporters to paying 3pp less. Against Asian suppliers, the UK’s advantage widens to between 8 and 25 points.

“Covered” is a big qualifier. Almost half of what the US buys from the 14 economies is exempt through the product annex: pharmaceuticals, civil aircraft, energy, smartphones and computers. Cars, steel, aluminium and the other Section 232 goods are also carved out, for every target except China. Only about 41% of these imports face the new rates, which is why the trade-weighted increases are much smaller than the headline rates.

Winners and losers around the world

Where I give a single number below, it is the central calibration. Ranges run from the Monte Carlo median to the central estimate.

The United States: paying for its own tariffs

The US is the clearest loser.

  • Under the proposal, US real income falls by 0.03–0.06%. That is despite about $34bn a year of extra tariff revenue: the higher prices US buyers pay for imports outweigh the revenue.
  • If talks fail and the fallback rates kick in (China at 40%, Korea, Taiwan and ASEAN at 25%), the loss doubles to 0.13%, even though revenue rises to $52bn.
  • If China and the EU retaliate, the loss grows to 0.20%.
  • The US loses in every scenario and in every one of the 5,000 draws.

The new tariffs mostly re-label duties that the Supreme Court struck down in February. A new legal basis does not change their economics.

China and its replacements

China loses 0.03–0.05% of real income under the proposal. If talks fail and the 40% fallback applies to all Chinese goods, the loss rises to 0.08–0.10%, and to 0.09–0.13% if China retaliates.

But China is not the biggest loser in proportional terms. Between January–May 2024 and January–May 2026, China’s share of US imports fell from 12.6% to 7.3%. Over the same period the other twelve targets rose from 26.7% to 36.4%. This is exactly the relocation that the “failure to address global excess capacity” findings take aim at, and the costs fall on the economies that took China’s place:

  • Cambodia loses 1.6%. Its exports are apparel with nothing in the exemption annex.
  • Vietnam loses 0.8% at the proposed 35%. If it signs a deal and gets 20% instead, the loss falls to 0.2%.
  • Malaysia (−0.14%) and Indonesia (−0.07%) lose too.

The biggest winners are the US’s neighbours left out of the action: Mexico (+0.20%), whose determination is pending, and Canada (+0.06%).

The EU: little change on income, more pressure on imports

The EU’s headline rate is unchanged at 15% all-in. In practice, it moves from the forced-labour cap of 10% to 15% on covered goods. Only about a third of EU exports to the US are exposed, so the trade-weighted increase is about 1.6pp.

  • Income barely moves. The central estimate is −0.004%, and the Monte Carlo median is essentially zero, with gains and losses equally likely.
  • Germany (−0.010%) and France (−0.013%) lose a little. Ireland gains a little (+0.013%): most of its exports are exempt, so its tariff rises less than its competitors’.
  • Retaliation hurts the EU most. If talks fail, the EU loses 0.012%. If it then suspends its 2026 tariff concessions on US goods and retaliates, it loses about 0.04%.

The bigger issue for Brussels is trade deflection. Chinese and Vietnamese goods priced out of the US market need to go somewhere. I estimate that $17bn (proposal) to $35bn (talks fail) could be redirected to the EU, equal to 1.1–2.2% of its imports from the 14 targets. This is several times what the UK faces.

The UK: winning by standing still

The UK is not targeted, and it already pays the forced-labour 10%. Its exporters therefore gain a preference margin over almost every competitor in the US market, without the UK doing anything.

UK outcomes relative to the tariff regime in force on 25 November 2026. Medians of 5,000 Monte Carlo draws. GE structural-gravity model, 81 economies, 2025 baseline.
Scenario UK real income, % (median) £bn a year (median) UK exports to the US, % (median)
Proposal as published +0.010 +0.30 +4.5
Deals signed (India 17%, Vietnam 20%, Singapore 10%) +0.008 +0.23 +3.5
Talks fail (fallback rates, China 40%) +0.021 +0.63 +9.8
Escalation (China and the EU retaliate) +0.012 +0.37 +6.5
UK drawn in at 15% +0.004 +0.12 +0.6
UK drawn in at 20% −0.004 −0.13 −4.7

The main points:

  • The gain is small but robust. Under the proposal, UK real income rises by 0.010% at the median, about £0.3bn a year. In the central calibration the gain is 0.016% (£0.5bn), and it is positive in all 5,000 draws.
  • It works through two channels.
    • US buyers switch from Chinese and Vietnamese suppliers to UK goods. UK exports to the US rise by 4.5% at the median and 6% (about £2.8bn) in the central run.
    • Asian goods priced out of the US flow to the UK instead. Imports from China rise by about 1.4–1.6%, and UK consumer prices fall slightly.
  • UK exports to the EU dip by about 0.35–0.5%, as some UK output is diverted to the US.
  • If talks fail, the gain doubles to about 0.02–0.03% (£0.6–0.9bn). This is the UK’s best case, but it comes with the largest fall in world income.
  • Being drawn in is the main risk. A UK determination at 15% would add only 5pp on covered goods, because the UK already pays 10%. Even so, it would wipe out most of the gain. At 20% the result turns negative: UK real income falls slightly and UK exports to the US fall by about 5%.

One caveat matters. The welfare gain depends on how the model treats trade imbalances. If trade deficits scale with output instead of staying fixed, it shrinks to about 0.002%. The trade diversion does not depend on this: UK exports to the US rise by about 6–9% under every set of assumptions I tested.

Which UK products gain

To see where the gains land, I used a product-level model at HS 6-digit level. US spending on each product is fixed, and buyers switch between suppliers as relative tariffs change. This model agrees with the GE model. UK exports to the US rise by $3.4bn (+6.2%) under the proposal, from a 2025 base of $54.8bn, and by $7.6bn if talks fail.

UK exports to the US, largest gains by HS chapter. Product-level model, US$, 2025 values.
HS chapter UK exports to US, 2025 ($bn) Gain, proposal ($m) Gain, % Gain if talks fail ($m)
84 Machinery and mechanical appliances 12.3 +690 +5.6 +1,489
90 Optical, measuring and medical instruments 3.4 +421 +12.3 +920
85 Electrical machinery and equipment 3.8 +377 +10.0 +835
38 Chemical products n.e.c. (incl. diagnostic reagents) 1.1 +187 +17.1 +385
39 Plastics and articles thereof 1.1 +162 +15.4 +399
29 Organic chemicals 0.9 +161 +18.5 +392
94 Furniture 1.0 +137 +14.0 +298
30 Pharmaceutical products 5.4 +121 +2.2 +293
33 Cosmetics and perfumery 0.5 +73 +14.9 +178
49 Printed books and other printed matter 0.4 +73 +17.7 +196

The pattern is clear. UK gains are biggest where it competes head-on with Chinese and Vietnamese suppliers, in goods that are neither exempt nor under Section 232. In the products where UK exporters gain, Chinese suppliers lose about $47bn of US sales and Vietnamese suppliers about $27bn. The UK picks up a slice of that. At the product level, the largest gains are in:

  • diagnostic and laboratory reagents: +$132m (+18%);
  • printed matter: books, brochures, leaflets, +$60m (+19%);
  • diesel engines: +$57m (+7%);
  • taps, valves and similar appliances: +$54m (+20%);
  • electrical machines and apparatus: +$46m (+14%);
  • plastic articles: +$38m (+18%), and cosmetics: +$32m (+14%);
  • medical technology: prosthetics (+$31m, +24%), lasers (+$31m, +17%), medical and surgical instruments (+$27m), optical analysis instruments (+$24m, +20%);
  • television cameras: +$27m (+36%), and gas filtration machinery: +$22m (+15%).

What hardly moves. Several of the UK’s largest exports to the US gain only 1–2%: cars ($8.2bn), pharmaceuticals ($5.4bn) and aircraft and parts ($2.4bn). Competitors’ cars, medicines and aircraft parts are also exempt or already under Section 232, so the new tariffs give the UK little extra advantage there.

The flip side: goods deflected to the UK

The same price wedge that helps UK exporters in the US also pushes Asian goods towards the UK. I estimate that $3bn (proposal) to $5bn (talks fail) of displaced sales could be redirected to the UK. That is only 0.4–0.7% of UK imports, and almost all of it comes from China and Vietnam.

The aggregate is small, but it is concentrated in a few product lines. If talks fail, the redirected volume reaches roughly 10–40% of UK imports in:

  • plastic builders’ ware, shutters and blinds from Vietnam (41% of UK imports of the product);
  • candles (15%) and concrete and artificial-stone articles (12%) from Vietnam;
  • hearing aids from Vietnam (10%). UK imports from Vietnam were already up 36% in January–May 2026;
  • hosiery and medical furniture from China (about 10% each);
  • wooden office furniture from Vietnam (10%). Imports were already up 69% in January–May 2026;
  • electric fans from China (9%). Imports were already up 94% in January–May 2026.

These are upper-bound estimates. Even so, these lines belong on a Trade Remedies Authority watch-list.

What it means for the UK

  1. Staying outside the net is the main UK interest, but the stakes are modest. The proposal is worth about £0.3–0.5bn a year. Being drawn in at 20% would turn that into a small loss.
    • USTR has shown that it can add economies: the forced-labour Section 301 already covers the UK, and Mexico and Norway are pending.
    • Before the 5 January deadline, the UK should argue on the record that it does not fit the profile these investigations are built on: persistent surpluses and low capacity utilisation. The UK runs a large goods deficit and has a small manufacturing share.
  2. The gain is a preference margin, and margins erode. Every competitor that cuts its rate through a deal, or wins product exclusions, takes some of it back. UK exporters of machinery, instruments and chemicals should prepare for the exclusion process.
  3. UK–EU coordination on trade defence makes sense. The EU faces several times the UK’s deflection pressure. Joint monitoring makes more sense than separate safeguards, especially for steel, aluminium and other sensitive products.
  4. The US is the biggest loser. The new tariffs mainly re-label duties that the Supreme Court struck down, and the US is worse off in every scenario.

Full analysis

The full report has the scenario design, product-level tariff construction, methodology, Monte Carlo and sensitivity results, deflection tables and caveats:

Section 301 “structural excess capacity” tariffs: what they entail and what they mean for the UK (full report, HTML)

Data and methods

  • Tariffs. I built the tariffs bottom-up at HS 6-digit level from the 14 USTR pre-publication notices and their annexes. I combined them with the forced-labour Section 301 tiers (91 FR 47717) and the official Section 232 product lists. The regime in force today comes from GTA’s modelled US tariff estimates. Tariffs that China, the EU and Canada now apply to US goods are included in every scenario.
  • GE model. A universal-gravity model (Allen, Arkolakis and Takahashi, 2020) of 81 economies, calibrated to 2025 bilateral goods trade from Trade Data Monitor. It excludes precious metals and uses θ = 5.14.
  • Uncertainty. I ran 5,000 Monte Carlo draws on Aston’s TAURUS cluster. They vary the trade and supply elasticities, how close the final rates come to the “up to” ceilings, the exemption mapping, Section 232 coverage and the weighting year.
  • Money values. £ figures apply the percentage changes to ONS 2025 GDP.
  • Caveats.
    • The GE model has one sector and no dynamics.
    • The final rates may be lower than the “up to” ceilings, and product exclusions will follow.
    • The deflection estimates are upper bounds.
    • The notices are pre-publication versions.

item.title: Trump Trade War Diary — Day 673
item.dc:creator: Oleksandr Shepotylo
item.description:
Topic: Section 301 “structural excess capacity” determinations, the legal rebuild of the reciprocal tariffs.

Eight and a half months ago USTR launched sixteen Section 301 investigations (Day 414). Today USTR Jamieson Greer announced determinations for 14 of the 16 economies. In every one of them, the acts, policies and practices “relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors” are found to be unreasonable and to burden or restrict U.S. commerce. That makes them actionable under Section 301(b).

Mexico and Norway got no determination “at this time”. Mexico is the largest single-country supplier of US imports ($517bn in 2025), so leaving it out is a political choice, not an analytical one. The process drew more than 1,070 written comments, and nearly 140 witnesses testified at the hearings of May 5–8, 2026.

Greer’s framing: trading partners pursued “industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression…”. The President therefore proposes action “to bring about the elimination of these unfair acts, policies, and practices.”

The press release gives only the headline rates. The real content is in the 14 pre-publication Federal Register notices (FRNs) and their product annexes. I downloaded all of them and went through them line by line. The numbers below are my own calculations from the FRNs and 2025 US trade data.

What is proposed

Each action is a tariff of “up to” X% on all goods from the economy, minus a list of exemptions. Each FRN also contains something the press release leaves out: an alternative rate.

  • Countries with a deal: the alternative is a higher fallback rate, which applies if “ongoing consultations and existing commitments are unsatisfactory”.
  • Countries without a deal (India, Vietnam, Singapore): it works the other way round. The headline rate is the stick. A lower rate applies “were [the country] to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade … responsive to the determinations”.
The 14 proposed Section 301 actions at a glance.
Economy US imports 2025 ($bn) Proposed rate (%) Alternative (%) IEEPA rate, Jul 2025 (%) Exempt: annex / S232 (% of imports) Exposed to proposed rate ($bn) Sectors singled out
European Union 586.8 15* 20* (fallback) 15 51 / 16 189.6 autos, chemicals, pharmaceuticals
China 292.5 20 (10 on Annex A) 40 (fallback) 20† 8 / – 270.0‡ 22 sectors: steel, aluminium, EVs, batteries, chips, solar, ships, robotics, textiles…
Taiwan 198.4 15* 25 (fallback) 20 84 / 6 20.3 electronics, semiconductors, telecoms
Vietnam 191.7 35 20 (if deal) 20 53 / 6 78.8 textiles, apparel, footwear, shipbuilding, cement, ICT
Japan 140.2 15* 20* (fallback) 15 28 / 44 39.7 autos, steel, semiconductors, optical fibre
Korea 121.7 15* 25* (fallback) 15 35 / 44 25.6 autos, semiconductors, petrochemicals
India 101.4 25 17 (if deal) 25 52 / 11 38.1 pharma, medical devices, steel, solar, ICT
Thailand 90.3 18 25 (fallback) 19 61 / 12 24.6 electronics, autos, machinery, electrical equipment
Malaysia 57.2 18 25 (fallback) 19 63 / 7 17.2 ICT, autos
Switzerland 41.7 15* 20* (fallback) 39 59 / 3 15.9 pharmaceuticals, steel, chemicals
Indonesia 34.4 18 25 (fallback) 19 25 / 8 23.1 textiles, apparel, mining & metals, renewables
Singapore 31.4 20 10 (if deal) 10 63 / 2 10.8 electronics, semiconductors, health, petrochemicals
Cambodia 15.1 18 25 (fallback) 19 4 / 11 12.9 apparel, solar, tyres
Bangladesh 9.3 18 20 (fallback) 20 0 / 0 9.3 ready-made garments
Total, 14 economies 1,912.2 775.9

* All-in rate, “net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs” (as in the 15% EU/Japan/Korea deals). The other rates are additional to MFN and net of existing Section 301 duties only. Taiwan’s 25% fallback is net of Section 301 only. † China: 10% reciprocal + 10% fentanyl after the Kuala Lumpur arrangement (EO 14358, Nov 2025). ‡ China: $167.5bn at the 20% rate plus $102.5bn of Annex A goods at 10%.

Sources: USTR pre-publication FRNs (25 Nov 2026); EO of 31 Jul 2025, Annex I. US imports are from TDM (HS6, 2025), excluding precious metals (7106, 7108, 7110, 7112, 7115) and special provisions (ch. 98–99). Annex exemptions are weighted by HTS-8 line shares within each HS6. Section 232 coverage comes from the official product lists.

The chart makes the main point clear. The “remedies” are the reciprocal-tariff deals, moved to a new legal basis.

  • EU, Japan and Korea get 15% all-in, exactly their 2025 framework rate.
  • Switzerland gets 15%. That is its November 2025 framework rate, not the punitive 39%.
  • Taiwan gets 15%, per the February 2026 Agreement on Reciprocal Trade.
  • China gets 20%. The FRN says explicitly that this “accounts for the commitments and 20 percent tariff rate announced as part of the Kuala Lumpur Joint Arrangement”.
  • Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Cambodia all have deals or frameworks, and they get 18%. That is one point below their old 19%, a small sweetener for having signed.

Each FRN footnotes the relevant bilateral agreement. The diagnosis is supposedly the same “structural excess capacity” everywhere, yet the rate follows deal status, not any measure of the harm. A Section 301 remedy is supposed to be set at whatever level gets the practice eliminated. These rates simply repeat the price agreed in the last negotiation.

What is exempted

The exemption annexes are close to identical across economies:

  • A common core of 2,114 HTS-8 lines appears unchanged in the annexes for Japan, Korea, India, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. China’s Annex A is exactly the same list, but for China it is a 10% tier, not an exemption.
    • The EU gets 44 extra lines.
    • Countries with signed agreements (Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Taiwan, Switzerland) get 86–156 extra lines. These are mostly agricultural products and inputs from their agreements.
  • The core list is essentially the old IEEPA Annex II plus later additions. It covers:
    • pharmaceuticals and their chemical inputs (641 lines in HS29 alone, roughly 700 lines restricted to pharmaceutical use);
    • civil aircraft and parts (roughly 550 lines restricted to civil aircraft);
    • energy (HS27), critical minerals and metals, and gold;
    • tropical agricultural products (coffee, spices, fruit, beef);
    • the electronics exemption of April 2025: computers (8471), smartphones (8517.13), network equipment and chips.
  • All economies except China also get a carve-out for goods already under Section 232. These are steel, aluminium, copper, passenger vehicles and light trucks, medium and heavy trucks and their parts, wood products, patented pharmaceuticals and semiconductors. The China FRN contains no Section 232 carve-out.
  • China’s Annex B (77 lines, fully exempt) comes from the U.S.-China Board of Trade “30-for-30” list: toys (9503, $9bn), fireworks, plastic tableware, bed and table linen, electric blankets.

A few numbers from 2025 US imports:

  • The 14 economies supplied $1.91 trillion, about 61% of US goods imports (excluding precious metals). Only about $776bn (41%) would face the proposed rates. The rest is exempt, either through the annex (mostly pharma and electronics) or through Section 232.
  • Exposure varies hugely.
    • Taiwan: 10%. Computers, servers and their parts are exempt, $132bn in 8471/8473 alone.
    • Korea and Japan: 21–28%. Autos and other goods are already under Section 232.
    • China 92%, Cambodia 85% and Bangladesh 99%. Garment exporters have nothing in the annex.
  • China’s 10% tier covers about $100bn. It is led by smartphones ($23.5bn), lithium-ion batteries ($11.7bn) and laptops ($8.6bn). The FRN names batteries as one of China’s excess-capacity sectors, yet batteries land in the low tier.
  • The extra duty is about $71bn a year at 2025 volumes: $28bn China, $18bn Vietnam, $9bn EU. This is far less than the headline rates suggest, because the new duty only tops up the forced-labour Section 301 that has applied to 60 economies since 24 July 2026. Once trade responds to the new tariffs, extra US tariff revenue is closer to $34bn.

Procedure and timing

  • Comments and hearings. Written comments and requests to appear are due January 5, 2027. Hearings start January 25, 2027 at the USITC. Comments go to separate dockets for each economy (e.g. China USTR-2026-0278, EU USTR-2026-0730). Requests to appear go to USTR-2026-0741.
  • No effective date yet. Realistically, the earliest implementation is Q1–Q2 2027.
  • An EU sunset. For the EU, USTR proposes that the action terminate on December 1, 2028. This matches the EU’s own Regulation (EU) 2026/1455, which grants tariff concessions on US goods from July 1, 2026 to December 31, 2029. The deal is being codified on both sides, with sunset dates attached.
  • China’s rate stacks on another 301. China’s 20% is net of the duty from yet another Section 301 action, on China’s failure to prohibit imports of goods made with forced labour (91 FR 47318, July 28, 2026). China declined USTR’s request for consultations.
  • A plurilateral option. USTR also asks for comments on whether to negotiate a plurilateral agreement on structural excess capacity, including with China. This is the only multilateral element in the whole exercise.

My observations

  1. This is the Supreme Court workaround. On February 20 the IEEPA tariffs were struck down. GTA’s modelled trade-weighted US tariff (top 1,000 flows) fell from about 10% in December 2025 to 5.8% on the day of the ruling. It stands at about 8.7% today (GTA US Tariff Estimates, model snapshot 2026-10-23). These 14 actions would rebuild most of the reciprocal-tariff wall on a statute that courts have treated with much more deference than IEEPA.
    • In HMTX Industries v. United States (25 Sep 2025), the Federal Circuit upheld the 2018 China Lists 3 and 4A. A cert petition (No. 25-1012) followed in February 2026.
    • Section 301 requires an investigation, a determination, notice and comment. The administration has now done all of that.
  2. “Excess capacity” has been stretched to mean “anything we don’t like about your macroeconomy”. The list of “unreasonable” practices includes:
    • Japan’s household investment promotion;
    • Singapore’s savings promotion policies that suppress domestic consumption;
    • Switzerland’s currency;
    • financial repression almost everywhere;
    • Taiwan’s past purchases of Russian feedstock;
    • for all of them, “failure to address global excess capacity”, i.e. buying Chinese inputs or hosting Chinese FDI.
    This is a saving-investment imbalance argument relabelled as an unfair trade practice. Comments on methodology were noted and set aside. They argued, for example, that low capacity utilisation can reflect the business cycle, and that trade surpluses reflect saving patterns.
  3. The remedy does not target the sectors in the diagnosis. The FRNs name steel, autos, semiconductors and pharma. Those are exactly the goods that are exempted, because they sit under Section 232 or in the annex. What is actually taxed is everything else: apparel from Bangladesh and Cambodia, furniture and footwear from Vietnam, machinery and consumer goods from Europe. The cost falls on garment workers in Dhaka and on US consumers, not on Chinese or Korean steel mills.
  4. It is a negotiating instrument with a legal wrapper. The stick-and-carrot structure shows the real objective: lock in the 2025–26 bilateral deals and keep leverage over them.
    • The sticks are fallback rates of up to 40% for China and 25% for Korea and Taiwan.
    • The carrots are deal rates of 17% for India, 20% for Vietnam and 10% for Singapore.
    • Korea’s 25% fallback matches the rate Trump threatened in January, when the Korean legislature had not passed the deal (Day 371).
  5. The WTO dimension is unchanged. Country-specific tariffs on all goods break MFN just as the IEEPA tariffs did. A WTO panel already found the 2018 China 301 tariffs inconsistent with GATT Articles I and II (DS543, 15 Sep 2020). The US appealed that ruling into the void left by the non-functioning Appellate Body, and nobody expects the WTO to matter here. The more interesting question is Mexico. Excluding the largest bilateral exporter while hitting Cambodia at 18% says a lot about where the USMCA review is.

The comment period runs over Christmas. Expect a flood of product-by-product exclusion requests. That is exactly how the deals will be renegotiated in 2027.

The UK angle

The UK is not on the list. That is good news for British exporters, but it comes with a catch.

  • The UK already pays 10% under the forced-labour Section 301. The new rates are net of existing Section 301 duties, so the excess-capacity action tops each target up to its headline rate and leaves the UK where it is.
  • That reverses the UK’s position against the EU. On a typical covered product, the UK goes from paying 2pp more than EU exporters to paying 3pp less.

I ran the proposal through a general-equilibrium trade model to see who gains and who loses: the US, China, the EU and the UK. I also looked at which UK product groups are likely to benefit. The results are in a companion post: Section 301 “excess capacity” tariffs: the US, China and Vietnam lose, the UK gains, if it stays outside.

item.title: Brussels Races the Clock: Europe’s Last-Minute Bid to Lock In a US Trade Deal
item.description:
The EU is accelerating negotiations toward a “rules and stability” pact with the US, aiming to close a deal by July that leans on regulatory alignment in digital, green and industrial policy rather than traditional tariff cuts. The goal is to insulate transatlantic commerce — worth around €1.2 trillion a year and supporting roughly 15 million jobs — from future tariff shocks, with steel and aluminium arrangements a particular point of vulnerability as they near expiration. Success would effectively let the EU and US set de facto global trade standards; failure would leave the UK, whose own US trade talks remain stalled, at a competitive disadvantage.

Originally published on Substack, May 6, 2026.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Trump’s 25% Tariff Shock on EU Cars: Trade Deal or Trade War?
item.description:
Trump has raised US tariffs on EU-imported vehicles from 15% to 25%, while exempting cars built by European brands at American plants — adding roughly $5,000 to the cost of a $50,000 imported car. The move is framed as a response to alleged EU non-compliance with earlier trade commitments and is designed to push European automakers to onshore production. It is likely to trigger EU retaliation against US agricultural and industrial exports, another marker of a transatlantic trade relationship becoming more unpredictable and more openly political.

Originally published on Substack, May 2, 2026.

Read the full piece →

item.title: The Return of Protectionism: Trump’s 2025 Tariffs and the Shifting Landscape of Global Trade
item.description:
Donald Trump’s return to the presidency in 2025 triggered the most significant protectionist surge since the 1930s, with the US average effective tariff reaching 18.2% by August 2025 — the highest level in 90 years. We synthesise economic theory and empirical evidence on the welfare effects of the new tariffs, analyse the current US trade measures, and quantify their impacts using a structural gravity model. Beyond the direct cost of the duties themselves, ongoing tariff uncertainty disrupts firms’ planning, forces costly duplication of supply chains, and triggers capital flight that undermines the very industrial goals protectionism claims to serve.

Published in: LSE Public Policy Review, 2026. With Jun Du and Yujie Shi.

Aston Research Explorer / ORCID

item.title: What steel tariffs reveal about the cost of going it alone
item.description:
Using trade data and economic modelling, this piece with Professor Jun Du examines the UK steel tariffs announced in March 2026. It finds the US tariffs already caused steel imports to fall 20% while consumer prices rose around 27%, with 70–80% of the cost passed on to downstream buyers. The UK’s roughly 300,000 downstream steel-using workers carry a heavier burden than its 30,000 primary steelmakers, and the piece argues the UK should coordinate its trade-defence policy with the EU rather than act alone — a joint approach could generate preferential gains worth roughly £482 million a year.

Originally published on UK in a Changing Europe, April 28, 2026.

Read the full piece →

item.title: NATO’s Hidden Dividend and the Avoidable Cost of U.S. Withdrawal
item.description:
NATO membership delivers economic benefits well beyond security: member states see bilateral trade rise by 12–27 percent. Drawing on our research, the piece estimates that a U.S. exit from the alliance would reduce American exports by about 16.1 percent (roughly $240 billion annually) and GDP by around 4 percent. The alliance’s economic integration, built through standardization agreements, interoperability requirements and long-term institutional trust, is a strategic asset that took 75 years to develop but could be lost far more rapidly if commitment erodes.

Co-authored with Philip Luck and Karen Jackson.

Originally published on CSIS, April 22, 2026.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Tariffs as Taxes at Home: How Trump-Era Trade Wars Still Shape Trade in 2026
item.description:
Trump-era tariffs functioned less like penalties on foreign exporters and more like taxes on American consumers: research finds pass-through rates of 80–100% to US buyers, only modest reshoring, and a small GDP drag with no real improvement in the structural trade deficit. Looking ahead, the piece warns tariffs risk becoming a permanent “leverage machine” in US trade strategy, posing ongoing risk to European sectors such as autos and green tech, while legal challenges to Section 232 continue to test the limits of presidential tariff authority.

Originally published on Substack, April 9, 2026.

Read the full piece →

item.title: From Steel to Pills: Trump’s Tariff Weapon Gets a Big Upgrade
item.description:
The Trump administration has expanded Section 232 national-security tariffs — originally reserved for steel and aluminium — to cover copper and patented pharmaceuticals. The US imports roughly $10–12 billion of copper and over $150 billion of drugs a year, with European and UK producers among the largest suppliers. The expansion signals that “national security” is becoming a catch-all justification for tariffs, raising the risk of allied retaliation and leaving firms unable to predict which sectors might be hit next, even close allies.

Originally published on Substack, April 7, 2026.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Beyond security: The trade implications of joining NATO
item.description:
Combining structural gravity methods with a staggered difference-in-differences design, we identify the causal effect of NATO membership on bilateral trade flows, separating it from the effect of a generic military alliance. NATO accession raises exports, with benefits that unfold gradually and intensify over time, coming through several channels: protecting and securing trade routes, lowering uncertainty and boosting cross-member investment, direct trade in military and military-related goods, and logistical support for military activity.

Working paper: SSRN Working Paper / BOFIT Discussion Paper, 2026. With Karen Jackson.

item.title: Brussels Says “Yes, But…” to Washington
item.description:
The European Parliament has conditionally approved a limited trade package with the US that lowers tariffs on select products while attaching strict safeguards. Unlike a comprehensive deal such as the old TTIP, this “mini-deal with a maxi-rulebook” prioritises EU regulatory autonomy on environment, labour and data protection over the size of the tariff cuts, which are modest given already-low starting rates. The transatlantic relationship behind it is enormous — around €1.3 trillion in 2023 trade and over 40% of global foreign investment stock — so Parliament’s insistence on embedding sustainability standards and enforceable protections sets a template that will shape how the West’s two largest economies structure trade going forward.

Originally published on Substack, March 27, 2026.

Read the full piece →

item.title: The £135 Question: Is Britain About to Tax Your Online Shopping Cart?
item.description:
The UK plans to eliminate its £135 customs relief threshold for low-value imports by March 2029, aligning with similar moves already under way in the EU and US. The change would bring hundreds of millions of annual parcels into scope for VAT and duties, and could raise prices on affected goods by 20–30%. Major retailers back the move, but business groups warn it could be inflationary and fall hardest on SMEs and lower-income consumers. It’s part of a broader global push to regulate cross-border e-commerce and capture tax revenue from the flood of cheap direct-to-consumer imports.

Originally published on Substack, March 24, 2026.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Steel Shield, Budget Blowout
item.description:
The UK government’s plan to double steel tariffs and tighten import quotas is meant to shield domestic steelmakers, but it risks pushing up construction costs sharply. Steel can account for 10–25% of materials costs on large infrastructure projects, and with the UK importing 60–70% of its construction steel, higher tariffs are likely to force expensive redesigns, scope cuts or delays — HS2, already under severe budget strain, is a prime example. The episode illustrates a broader tension in trade policy: protecting an upstream industry (steel) effectively taxes downstream sectors (construction, infrastructure), potentially undercutting the very strategic goals the tariffs are meant to serve.

Originally published on Substack, March 23, 2026.

Read the full piece →

item.title: After the Court slapped down Trump’s tariffs, USTR is trying to build a sturdier tariff machine
item.description:
The Trump administration has opened Section 301 investigations against 16 trading partners, targeting alleged “structural excess capacity” in manufacturing. Rather than imposing tariffs immediately — the approach courts recently blocked — this procedural route builds a formal record through hearings and public comment before any action is taken. The notice conflates genuine overcapacity with ordinary bilateral trade surpluses and wage differentials, two economically distinct things, and the target list spans China, EU members, Japan, India and others across electronics, autos, chemicals and steel. The effect is a reusable legal doctrine for tariffing any economy running a manufacturing surplus, regardless of the underlying cause.

Originally published on Substack, March 12, 2026.

Read the full piece →

item.title: Trump Trade War Diary — Day 414
item.description:
Being defeated in the Supreme Court, Trump is now trying to find ways to keep his tariffs in place. His trade representative, Jamieson Greer initiated a section 301 investigation, which is available at link.

This document is a USTR Federal Register notice launching Section 301 investigations into whether the acts, policies, and practices of certain economies create or maintain structural excess capacity and overproduction in manufacturing. It is not a final tariff announcement; it starts an investigation process and opens the door to hearings and public comments. The notice argues that some trading partners have built production capacity beyond what domestic and global demand can justify, causing overproduction, persistent trade surpluses, unused capacity, and pressure on U.S. manufacturing, investment, and jobs.

USTR says the problem is linked to policy distortions such as subsidies, suppressed wages, state-owned or state-controlled firms, market-access barriers, weak labor/environmental protections, subsidized lending, and currency or financial practices. It also frames trade surpluses with the United States as a sign that foreign excess production is being exported into the U.S. market, directly or indirectly through third countries.

The investigations cover China, the EU, Singapore, Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Mexico, Japan, and India. The notice gives economy-specific examples: China is presented as the biggest case, with a 2025 global goods trade surplus above $1.2 trillion and low capacity utilization; the EU is cited for a large goods surplus and Germany/Ireland are highlighted within it; Mexico, Japan, and India are singled out for large bilateral surpluses with the U.S. and sectoral excess capacity, especially in autos, steel, solar, petrochemicals, and related manufacturing.

Procedurally, USTR initiated the cases on March 11, 2026. Written comments and requests to appear were to open on March 17, 2026; comments and hearing requests are due by April 15, 2026; hearings begin May 5, 2026; and rebuttal comments are due seven days after the hearing closes. USTR specifically asks for evidence on whether the identified practices are unreasonable or discriminatory, whether they burden U.S. commerce, and what remedies should be taken, including tariff and non-tariff actions.

item.title: Europe Flirts with a “Buy European” Era
item.description:
The EU is adopting a “Buy European” policy that favours EU-made products in government procurement and industrial support for strategic sectors such as defence, clean tech, and AI. The shift reflects Europe’s declining share of global manufacturing (down from 25% to 20%), competition from China’s dominance in sectors like solar panels and batteries, and the aggressive subsidies of the US Inflation Reduction Act. Framed as a security measure rather than protectionism, the policy could nonetheless squeeze out US and UK suppliers and risks triggering retaliation — another sign of the drift from open-market globalisation toward bloc-based economic strategy.

Originally published on Substack, February 13, 2026.

item.title: Trump Trade War Diary — Day 374
item.description:
On Aircraft and the Art of Regulatory Retaliation

The US has announced it will decertify Bombardier aircraft and threatens 50% tariffs on all Canadian planes—unless Canada certifies Gulfstream jets “immediately.” This is a notable shift in trade war tactics. The blunt universal tariff—the economic equivalent of shouting at weather—has given way to something more precise: weaponised certification. The framing is instructive. Canada’s certification process isn’t “illegal”; it’s simply Canadian. Different country, different timeline. This has been true since approximately the invention of countries. But by presenting decertification as response rather than aggression, Washington shifts the narrative.

Why aircraft? Bombardier is a crown jewel of Canadian manufacturing, politically impossible to abandon. Meanwhile, Canada has been diversifying trade toward the EU and Asia—reducing its dependence on US markets. Targeting aerospace sends a clear message: alternatives have costs. The deeper problem is that using safety certification as a trade weapon rather undermines the concept of mutual recognition that makes international aviation function. If every country’s airworthiness decisions become bargaining chips, we end up with planes certified to fly everywhere except the places they need to go.

Somewhere in Toulouse, Airbus executives are watching with the quiet satisfaction of people who didn’t start the fire but remembered to bring marshmallows.

item.title: Trump Trade War Diary — Day 371
item.description:
Over the last several months, there were no significant changes in the trade policy diary, until post -New Year period, when Trump announced a new wave of tariff threats asking for political consessions from several countries.

On January 12, 2026 He demanded that all countries stopped trading with Iran, threatening to impose 25% tariffs on all imports from countries that do not comply with this demand.

On January 17 , 2026 He posted this photo, proclaiming himself and he started assault on Denmark demanding it to seed Greenland to US, threatening to impose 25% tariffs on all imports from Denmark if it does not comply with this demand.

To follow through, he declared now infamous “Greenland Tariffs” later in the day promising 10% tariff on Feeb 1 on eight European countries, who sent troops to Greenland as part of NATO mission, and 25% tariff on the same countries by June, if Denmark does not agree to sell Greenland to US. The sending of troops to Greenland was a symbolic move to demonstrate the solidarity, it was tiny military deployment, UK for instance sent only 1 person and Germany withdraw its troops right after the announcement of tariffs. Volodymyr Zelensky called it rather pathetic move, demonstartion of European weakness.

The both threat of tariffs on Iran and European countries demonstrated that Trump is going to use tariffs as a political tool to achieve his geopolitical objectives, rather than for trade policy purposes. It is vulnerable to the decision of the US supreme court who will deliver its verdict on the legality of tariffs imposed by Trump without approval of the US Congress. If the court decides that Trump exceeded his authority, all tariffs imposed by him may be declared illegal and removed. So the legal ground is shacky, but it creates political drama and increase uncertainty for businesses. People say that Trump TACO, which is true until it is not, as in the case of Venezuela, where he caputred its president Maduro and delivered him to the US court in New York.

Trump reversed his position on Greenland at Davos conference, on Jan 21 2026 saying that the issue is resolved after the conversation with NATO secretary general Mark Rutte. It is a temporary truce and the story will continue. But for now, the threat of quick NATO disintegration and occupation of Denmakr territory by US is removed.

He continued putting preassure on countries including Canada over its trade agreement with China on Jan 24, threatening to impose 100% if Canada if it signs the deal.

Finally, today Jan 27, 2026 he announced an increase in tariffs on Korea from 15 to 25% because Korea’s Legislature hasn’t inacted the Korea-US deal. .

At the same time other countries and trade blocks are deleveraging from US, with Canada signing a trade deal with China and with EU on SAFE framework, for EU weapons procurement. EU singing deals with MERCOSUR and India, and UK turning towards China.

item.title: Greenland Tariffs and UK Trade: Building Deterrence beyond Tariffs
item.description:
On 17 January 2026 the Trump administration threatened 10% tariffs on eight European countries, including the UK, that had sent military personnel to Greenland. The threat was withdrawn four days later and no tariffs were imposed — but the episode showed that economic coercion can come from security allies, not only from strategic rivals.

Key findings

  • We model eight scenarios: 10% and 25% US tariffs, each with and without UK and EU retaliation.
  • UK retaliation leaves the UK worse off in every scenario — not retaliating is a dominant strategy, and coordinated UK–EU tariff retaliation is the worst outcome for Britain.
  • Europe’s leverage lies elsewhere: the US runs a €148 billion annual services surplus with the EU, and mutual EU–US FDI stocks exceed €5.3 trillion.
  • US tariff revenue reached $264 billion in 2025, creating fiscal incentives that trade negotiations alone may not unwind.
  • China, India, Brazil and Canada are the most likely destinations for UK exports displaced from the US.

Policy recommendations

  1. Recognise fiscal extraction — tariff revenue creates lasting incentives, especially when security-dependent allies cannot credibly retaliate.
  2. Build UK–EU coordination on non-tariff tools — services, investment, procurement and regulation offer pressure points where Europe can impose asymmetric costs. The UK should seek observer or associate status in EU Anti-Coercion Instrument deliberations and coordinate on investment screening.
  3. Treat China trade as portfolio diversification — separate genuine security risks from commercial opportunities rather than decoupling across the board.

For the accompanying commentary, see Europe has five options for responding to Trump’s Greenland threats (The Conversation, January 2026).

Policy brief and working paper: Centre for Business Prosperity, Aston University, January 2026. With Jun Du.
